claim: A multicenter study of 60 healthy humans was conducted, with half receiving general anesthesia for 3 hours and half serving as awake controls.
source: To address this question, we conducted a multicenter study of 60 healthy humans, half of whom received general anesthesia for 3 hr and half of whom served as awake controls.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the study design with specific numbers of participants and conditions.

claim: Just prior to the recovery of consciousness, frontal-parietal dynamics returned to baseline.
source: We found that, just prior to the recovery of consciousness, frontal-parietal dynamics returned to baseline.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from the study's EEG measurements.

claim: Cognitive reconstitution after anesthesia evolved over time.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, cognitive reconstitution after anesthesia evolved over time.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding consistent with the hypothesis.

claim: Executive function returned first after anesthesia, contrary to the hypothesis.
source: Contrary to our hypothesis, executive function returned first.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding contradicted the original hypothesis.

claim: Early engagement of prefrontal cortex in recovery of consciousness and cognition is consistent with global neuronal workspace theory.
source: Early engagement of prefrontal cortex in recovery of consciousness and cognition is consistent with global neuronal workspace theory.
evidence: The abstract provides this interpretation of the findings in relation to theory.

claim: General anesthesia represents a controlled and reproducible method to perturb consciousness and cognition that is amenable to systematic observations of the recovery process.
source: General anesthesia, by contrast, represents a controlled and reproducible method by which to perturb consciousness and cognition that is also amenable to systematic observations of the recovery process.
evidence: The introduction presents this as a rationale for using general anesthesia in the study.

claim: Animal studies suggest that general anesthetics have the potential to immediately and persistently impair cognition in the post-anesthetic period.
source: Studying recovery of cognition after general anesthesia in humans is also of particular importance because animal studies suggest that general anesthetics have the potential to immediately and persistently impair cognition in the post-anesthetic period (Culley et al., 2004; Valentim et al., 2008; Carr et al., 2011; Callaway et al., 2012; Zurek et al., 2012; Jevtovic-Todorovic et al., 2013; Zurek et al., 2014; Avidan and Evers, 2016; Jiang et al., 2017)
evidence: The introduction cites multiple animal studies supporting this claim.

claim: Hundreds of millions of surgical patients undergo general anesthesia each year.
source: creating a potential public health concern for the hundreds of millions of surgical patients undergoing general anesthesia each year (Weiser et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a reference for this epidemiological claim.

claim: The study involved 30 healthy volunteers at three centers who were administered deep general anesthesia using isoflurane for 3 hours.
source: To improve scientific understanding of recovery of consciousness and cognition after anesthetic-induced unconsciousness, we studied 30 healthy volunteers at three centers who were administered deep general anesthesia using isoflurane for 3 hr, with cognitive testing conducted at pre-anesthetic baseline as well as every 30 min for 3 hr after return of consciousness (Figure 1).
evidence: The introduction describes the experimental design with specific details and references Figure 1.

claim: The hypothesis was that post-anesthetic recovery would be an extended process commencing with return of responsiveness and concluding with return of executive function.
source: We hypothesized that post-anesthetic recovery would be an extended process rather than a single point, commencing with return of responsiveness and concluding with return of executive function.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the study hypothesis.

claim: There is evidence that neurologic recovery from general anesthesia occurs in a caudal-to-rostral direction.
source: We hypothesized that executive function would be the last to recover because there is evidence that neurologic recovery from general anesthesia occurs in a caudal-to-rostral direction (Långsjö et al., 2012; Reshef et al., 2019)
evidence: The introduction cites prior studies supporting this directional pattern of recovery.

claim: Isoflurane anesthesia was chosen because of its heterogeneous molecular targets affecting multiple neural systems.
source: Isoflurane anesthesia was chosen because of its heterogeneous molecular targets, which affect multiple neural systems, and because its slower offset compared to other anesthetics would allow us to observe differential recovery of function (Hemmings et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction provides the rationale for choosing isoflurane with a citation.

claim: Isoflurane has a slower offset compared to other anesthetics, allowing observation of differential recovery of function.
source: Isoflurane anesthesia was chosen because of its heterogeneous molecular targets, which affect multiple neural systems, and because its slower offset compared to other anesthetics would allow us to observe differential recovery of function (Hemmings et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction explains the pharmacokinetic rationale for choosing isoflurane.

claim: Clinical observations and research comparing recovery from isoflurane vs. propofol support the interpretation that halogenated ethers have more profound effects on neural dynamics.
source: Clinical observations as well as clinical research comparing recovery from isoflurane vs. propofol support this interpretation (Pollard et al., 1994; Geng et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites clinical studies supporting this comparison.

claim: The Motor Praxis Task measures sensorimotor speed and depends upon function of visual and sensorimotor cortices.
source: The Motor Praxis Task (MP) measures sensorimotor speed and validates that volunteers have sufficient command of the computer interface. Participants were instructed to click on squares that appear randomly on the screen, with each successive square smaller and thus more difficult to track. The test depends upon function of visual and sensorimotor cortices (Gur et al., 2001; Gur et al., 2010; Neves et al., 2014).
evidence: The methods section describes the test and cites studies supporting the neuroanatomical basis.

claim: The Psychomotor Vigilance Test measures reaction times to visual stimuli presented at random inter-stimulus intervals over 3 minutes.
source: The Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) measures a volunteer's reaction times (RT) to visual stimuli that are presented at random inter-stimulus intervals over 3 min (Basner et al., 2011).
evidence: The methods section describes the PVT with a citation.

claim: In the well-rested state, right frontoparietal cortical regions are active during the Psychomotor Vigilance Test.
source: In the well-rested state, or whenever sustained attention performance is optimal, right frontoparietal cortical regions are active during this task.
evidence: The methods section describes the neuroanatomical correlates of the PVT.

claim: With sleep deprivation, there is increased activation of default-mode networks during the Psychomotor Vigilance Test, which is considered a compensatory mechanism.
source: Conversely, with sleep deprivation and other suboptimal performance, studies demonstrate increased activation of default-mode networks during this task, which is considered to be a compensatory mechanism (Drummond et al., 2005).
evidence: The methods section cites a study supporting this neural mechanism.

claim: The Digit-Symbol Substitution Task primarily recruits the temporal cortex, prefrontal cortex, and motor cortex.
source: The DSST primarily recruits the temporal cortex, prefrontal cortex, and motor cortex.
evidence: The methods section describes the neuroanatomical basis of the DSST.

claim: Activation of frontoparietal cortices during DSST performance has been interpreted as reflecting both on-board processing in working memory and low-level visual search.
source: Activation of frontoparietal cortices during DSST performance has been interpreted as reflecting both on-board processing in working memory and low-level visual search (Usui et al., 2009).
evidence: The methods section cites a study interpreting the neural correlates of DSST.

claim: The Fractal 2-Back is a well-validated task that robustly activates dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, cingulate, and hippocampus.
source: The F2B is a well-validated task that robustly activates dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, cingulate, and hippocampus (Ragland et al., 2002).
evidence: The methods section cites a study validating the neural correlates of the F2B.

claim: Visual object learning tasks depend upon frontal and bilateral anterior medial temporal cortices as well as the hippocampus.
source: Visual object learning tasks have been shown to depend upon frontal and bilateral anterior medial temporal cortices as well as the hippocampus (Jackson and Schacter, 2004).
evidence: The methods section cites a study supporting the neuroanatomical basis of VOLT.

claim: The Abstract Matching test evaluates abstraction and cognitive flexibility and depends upon the prefrontal cortex.
source: The abstract matching paradigm evaluates abstraction and cognitive flexibility and depends upon the prefrontal cortex (Berman et al., 1995).
evidence: The methods section cites a study supporting the neuroanatomical basis of AM.

claim: The average age of all study participants was 27 (±4.5) years, with 50% females.
source: The average age of all study participants was 27 (±4.5) years, with 50% females.
evidence: The results section provides demographic data for the study participants.

claim: There were no adverse events during the course of the study or at 1-week follow up.
source: There were no adverse events during the course of the study or at 1-week follow up at the completion of the study.
evidence: The results section reports safety outcomes.

claim: In anesthetized volunteers, the accuracy and speed of all six cognitive tests were significantly impaired compared with the pre-anesthetic baseline assessments.
source: In anesthetized volunteers (with correction for learning based on results from tests taken at corresponding times by the non-anesthetized controls), the accuracy and speed of all six cognitive tests were significantly impaired compared with the pre-anesthetic baseline assessments (all twelve statistical tests yielded p<0.008, with adjustments for multiple comparisons).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings on cognitive impairment.

claim: There were statistically significant differences in the rates of recovery of the six cognitive domains, both with regard to their accuracy and speed.
source: Based on likelihood ratio tests, there were statistically significant differences in the rates of recovery of the six cognitive domains, both with regard to their accuracy and speed (p<0.05).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings on differential recovery rates.

claim: Recovery of cognition is a process that appears to evolve over time rather than one that occurs simultaneously.
source: Hence, recovery of cognition is a process that appears to evolve over time rather than one that occurs simultaneously.
evidence: The results section draws this conclusion from the statistical analyses.

claim: For accuracy, the probability was high (95%) that recovery of Abstract Matching occurred more than 30 minutes before Fractal 2-Back.
source: For accuracy (Figure 2), the probability was high that (i) recovery of AM occurred more than 30 min before NBCK (95%), DSST (77%), VOLT (72%), and MP (65%)
evidence: The results section presents Bayesian probability estimates with reference to Figure 2.

claim: At 3 hours after recovery of consciousness in the anesthetized group, accuracies in five out of six tests were not statistically significantly different from the control group.
source: At 3 hr after ROC in the anesthetized group, accuracies in five out of six tests were not statistically significantly different from the control group.
evidence: The results section presents statistical comparisons between groups at 3 hours.

claim: There remained a significant (p<0.001), albeit small, difference in accuracy performance between the anesthetized and the control group on the Visual Object Learning Test at 3 hours.
source: There remained a significant (p<0.001), albeit small, difference in accuracy performance between the anesthetized and the control group on the VOLT at 3 hr.
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for VOLT at 3 hours.

claim: Within 3 hours of return of consciousness, the anesthetized group returned to an accuracy level that was not substantially different from that of participants who were not anesthetized.
source: Overall, within 3 hr of return of consciousness, the anesthetized group returned to an accuracy level that was not substantially different from that of participants who were not anesthetized.
evidence: The results section summarizes the overall accuracy findings.

claim: At 3 hours after recovery of consciousness in the anesthetized group, speed in two (Motor Praxis and Psychomotor Vigilance Test) out of six tests were not statistically significantly different from the control group.
source: At 3 hr after ROC in the anesthetized group, speed in two (MP and PVT) out of six tests were not statistically significantly different from the control group.
evidence: The results section presents statistical comparisons for speed at 3 hours.

claim: There remained significant (p<0.001) differences between the anesthetized and the control group in speed performance on four tests (VOLT, NBCK, AM, DSST) at 3 hours.
source: There remained significant (p<0.001), albeit small, differences between the anesthetized and the control group in speed performance on four (VOLT, NBCK, AM, DSST) tests at 3 hr.
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for speed at 3 hours.

claim: Permutation entropy demonstrated significant differences associated with behavioral states (F9, 86 = 42.423, p<0.001).
source: Using a linear mixed model, the PE demonstrated significant differences associated with behavioral states (F9, 86 = 42.423, p<0.001), brain regions (F1, 257 = 4.275, p=0.040), and the interaction between them (F9, 85 = 2.750, p=0.007).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings from linear mixed model analysis of PE.

claim: Frontal permutation entropy decreased at propofol-induced loss of consciousness.
source: As compared to the baseline condition of eyes-closed resting state, frontal PE decreased at propofol-induced loss of consciousness (LOC)
evidence: The results section describes changes in frontal PE at LOC.

claim: Frontal permutation entropy further decreased during maintenance of the anesthetized state with isoflurane anesthesia (p<0.001, -0.160 [-0.185 to -0.135], maintenance vs. EC1).
source: further decreased during maintenance of the anesthetized state with isoflurane anesthesia (p<0.001,–0.160 [-0.185 to −0.135], maintenance vs. EC1)
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for frontal PE during maintenance.

claim: Frontal permutation entropy returned to or even exceeded the baseline level just before the recovery of consciousness (p=0.002, 0.036 [0.018 to 0.055], pre-ROC vs. EC1).
source: and returned to or even exceeded the baseline level just before the recovery of consciousness (ROC) (p=0.002, 0.036 [0.018 to 0.055], pre-ROC vs. EC1) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for frontal PE before ROC with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Posterior permutation entropy did not show significant changes at loss of consciousness but was decreased during the maintenance phase (p<0.001, -0.110 (-0.135 to -0.085), maintenance vs. EC1).
source: Posterior PE did not show significant changes at LOC but was decreased during the maintenance phase (p<0.001,–0.110 (-0.135 to −0.085), maintenance vs. EC1), and then returned to baseline level just before ROC (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for posterior PE with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Frontal channels demonstrated significantly higher permutation entropy values compared to posterior channels at the eyes-closed resting state directly after emergence (EC2, p=0.002, 0.032 [0.016 to 0.048], frontal vs. posterior).
source: The topographic maps of PE exhibited region-specific patterns, in which frontal channels demonstrated significantly higher PE values as compared to posterior channels at the eyes-closed resting state directly after emergence (EC2, p=0.002, 0.032 [0.016 to 0.048], frontal vs. posterior) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for regional differences in PE with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Lempel-Ziv complexity demonstrated significant state-dependent differences (F9, 50 = 59.364, p<0.001).
source: The LZC demonstrated significant state-dependent differences (F9, 50 = 59.364, p<0.001).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings from analysis of LZC.

claim: Lempel-Ziv complexity declined at loss of consciousness and decreased further during the maintenance phase (p<0.001, -0.258 [-0.285 to -0.231], maintenance vs. EC1).
source: As compared to baseline consciousness, LZC declined at LOC and decreased further during the maintenance phase (p<0.001,–0.258 [-0.285 to −0.231], maintenance vs. EC1), returning to baseline level just before ROC (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for LZC with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Both the local (permutation entropy) and global (Lempel-Ziv complexity) metrics of cortical dynamics recover just as the brain is recovering consciousness.
source: Thus, both the local (PE) and global (LZC) metrics of cortical dynamics recover just as the brain is recovering consciousness.
evidence: The results section draws this conclusion from the EEG findings.

claim: The non-anesthetized control group showed no differences among the seven resting-state eyes-closed epochs.
source: Additionally, as expected, the non-anesthetized control group showed no differences among the seven resting-state eyes-closed epochs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section presents findings for the control group with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: There was no evidence that the EEG measures during EC1 are associated with the impairment in accuracy or response time for all tasks.
source: We found no evidence that the EEG measures during EC1 is associated with the impairment in accuracy or response time for all tasks (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The results section presents findings from correlation analysis with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The Lempel-Ziv complexity during Maintenance showed some correlation with the impairment of response time for Motor Praxis (r = 0.522, p=0.004) and DSST (r = 0.446, p=0.016) tasks.
source: Of note, the LZC during Maintenance showed some correlation with the impairment of response time for MP (r = 0.522, p=0.004) and DSST (r = 0.446, p=0.016) tasks (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The results section presents correlation findings with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Both the frontal permutation entropy and Lempel-Ziv complexity were found to be weakly correlated with the impairment of accuracy for DSST task (r = 0.381, p=0.046 and r = 0.479, p=0.011).
source: Moreover, both the frontal PE and LZC were found to be weakly correlated with the impairment of accuracy for DSST task (r = 0.381, p=0.046 and r = 0.479, p=0.011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The results section presents correlation findings with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Time of day significantly affected inactivity in both groups (F129, 6867 = 46.24, p<0.0001).
source: As expected, time of day significantly affected inactivity in both groups (F129, 6867 = 46.24, p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings from actigraphy analysis.

claim: Cosinar analysis demonstrated that peak inactivity occurred between 3 and 4 am for both groups.
source: Cosinar analysis demonstrated that peak inactivity occurred between 3 and 4 am for both groups.
evidence: The results section presents findings from Cosinar analysis of actigraphy data.

claim: Over the week prior to the study day, there were no significant differences between the participants who would subsequently be anesthetized and those who would not (F1, 6865 = 3.70, p>0.05).
source: Importantly, two-way ANOVA analysis revealed that over the week prior to the study day, there were no significant differences between the participants who would subsequently be anesthetized and those who would not (F1, 6865 = 3.70, p>0.05).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings comparing groups before the study day.

claim: There were no significant interactions between time and group in the week prior to the study day (F149, 6865 = 1.18, p>0.05).
source: Moreover, there were no significant interactions between time and group (F149, 6865 = 1.18, p>0.05).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for time-group interactions before the study day.

claim: Actigraphy revealed a small yet statistically significant effect of anesthetic exposure, accounting for only 0.19% of the total variance (F1, 3576 = 12.55, p=0.0004).
source: Actigraphy revealed a small yet statistically significant effect of anesthetic exposure, accounting for only 0.19% of the total variance (F1, 3576 = 12.55, p=0.0004).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for the effect of anesthesia on actigraphy.

claim: The effect of anesthetic exposure on actigraphy was attributable to an increase in inactivity in the isoflurane-exposed volunteers during the initial 2 hours of the early evening.
source: This was attributable to an increase in inactivity in the isoflurane-exposed volunteers during the initial 2 hr of the early evening (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section describes the temporal pattern of the actigraphy effect with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Activity patterns were not distinguishable between groups after the initial 2 hours of the early evening.
source: Activity patterns were not distinguishable after that time period.
evidence: The results section describes the temporal limitation of the actigraphy effect.

claim: Time remained as a highly significant predictor of inactivity accounting for 42% of the variance (F77, 3576 = 35.78, p<0.0001) after the study day.
source: As before the study day, time remained as a highly significant predictor of inactivity accounting for 42% of the variance (F77, 3576 = 35.78, p<0.0001).
evidence: The results section presents statistical findings for time as a predictor after the study day.

claim: This is the most comprehensive and controlled study assessing cognitive recovery from the anesthetized state in healthy humans.
source: This is the most comprehensive and controlled study assessing cognitive recovery from the anesthetized state in healthy humans.
evidence: The discussion section makes this claim about the study's significance.

claim: The investigation was unique in that the length and depth of general anesthesia was consistent with surgical conditions but the experimental paradigm did not include any surgical intervention.
source: Although there have been numerous studies of recovery from anesthetic-induced unconsciousness (Långsjö et al., 2012; Purdon et al., 2013; Chennu et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2018; Banks et al., 2020; Scheinin et al., 2021), our investigation was unique in that the length and depth of general anesthesia was consistent with surgical conditions but the experimental paradigm did not include any surgical intervention.
evidence: The discussion section describes the unique aspects of the study design with citations to prior work.

claim: Reconstitution of cognition after general anesthesia is a process that unfolds over time rather than a discrete, singular event.
source: We have demonstrated that reconstitution of cognition after general anesthesia is a process that unfolds over time rather than a discrete, singular event.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: Executive function was found to recover early, whereas tests of processing speed, attention, and reaction time had a more prolonged recovery.
source: Cognitive recovery also follows a counterintuitive sequence. Executive function was found to recover early, whereas tests of processing speed, attention, and reaction time had a more prolonged recovery.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the sequence of cognitive recovery.

claim: EEG-based measures of cortical dynamics return to baseline just prior to the recovery of consciousness after general anesthesia.
source: Furthermore, EEG-based measures of cortical dynamics return to baseline just prior to the recovery of consciousness after general anesthesia, with entropy in frontal cortex statistically significantly higher than posterior cortex just after emergence.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the EEG findings.

claim: Entropy in frontal cortex was statistically significantly higher than posterior cortex just after emergence.
source: Furthermore, EEG-based measures of cortical dynamics return to baseline just prior to the recovery of consciousness after general anesthesia, with entropy in frontal cortex statistically significantly higher than posterior cortex just after emergence.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the regional EEG findings.

claim: There were not strong predictors of cognitive recovery based on EEG dynamics.
source: There were not, however, strong predictors of cognitive recovery based on EEG dynamics.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the lack of strong EEG-cognition correlations.

claim: Sleep-wake activity patterns are essentially unperturbed after anesthetic exposure.
source: Finally, sleep-wake activity patterns are essentially unperturbed after anesthetic exposure.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the actigraphy findings.

claim: The finding that performance on the abstract matching test displayed more robust recovery than other cognitive functions indicates that there is early engagement of prefrontal cortex after recovery of consciousness.
source: However, the finding that performance on the abstract matching test displayed more robust recovery than other cognitive functions indicates that there is early engagement of prefrontal cortex after recovery of consciousness.
evidence: The discussion section interprets the cognitive findings in terms of prefrontal cortex engagement.

claim: EEG analysis demonstrated that both anterior and posterior cortices were active in association with recovery of consciousness.
source: Furthermore, EEG analysis demonstrated that both anterior and posterior cortices were active in association with recovery of consciousness, although there was no statistically significant relationship between neurophysiologic complexity in prefrontal cortex and subsequent executive function performance.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the EEG findings regarding cortical activity.

claim: There was no statistically significant relationship between neurophysiologic complexity in prefrontal cortex and subsequent executive function performance.
source: Furthermore, EEG analysis demonstrated that both anterior and posterior cortices were active in association with recovery of consciousness, although there was no statistically significant relationship between neurophysiologic complexity in prefrontal cortex and subsequent executive function performance.
evidence: The discussion section reports the lack of correlation between prefrontal EEG and executive function.

claim: The results are aligned with the theoretical framework of global neuronal workspace theory.
source: Collectively, our results are aligned with the theoretical framework of global neuronal workspace theory, which attempts to describe the neurocognitive mechanisms of conscious access (Dehaene et al., 1998; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Mashour et al., 2020).
evidence: The discussion section interprets the findings in relation to global neuronal workspace theory with citations.

claim: Access consciousness refers to the broad cognitive availability of sensory information, which often is measured based on report or task performance.
source: Access consciousness refers to the broad cognitive availability of sensory information, which often is measured based on report or task performance (as in this study), and is distinct from phenomenal consciousness, which has been defined as experience itself and hypothesized to be independent of post-perceptual processing in anterior cortex (Block, 2005; Raccah et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion section defines access consciousness with citations.

claim: Phenomenal consciousness has been defined as experience itself and hypothesized to be independent of post-perceptual processing in anterior cortex.
source: Access consciousness refers to the broad cognitive availability of sensory information, which often is measured based on report or task performance (as in this study), and is distinct from phenomenal consciousness, which has been defined as experience itself and hypothesized to be independent of post-perceptual processing in anterior cortex (Block, 2005; Raccah et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion section defines phenomenal consciousness with citations.

claim: According to workspace theory, a reverberant network that includes both prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex serves to sustain, amplify, and make available neural representations.
source: According to workspace theory, a reverberant network that includes both prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex serves to sustain, amplify, and make available neural representations, with a 'broadcasting' effect that allows access by otherwise non-conscious cognitive processors (Mashour et al., 2020).
evidence: The discussion section describes global neuronal workspace theory with a citation.

claim: The active frontal-parietal networks at return of consciousness and early recovery of a cognitive test associated with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are consistent with at least a partially reintegrated global neuronal workspace.
source: The active frontal-parietal networks at return of consciousness and early recovery of a cognitive test associated with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are consistent with at least a partially reintegrated global neuronal workspace.
evidence: The discussion section interprets the findings in relation to global neuronal workspace theory.

claim: A fully intact workspace requires exquisite temporal coordination.
source: However, a fully intact workspace requires exquisite temporal coordination.
evidence: The discussion section describes a requirement of the global neuronal workspace.

claim: The differential temporal recovery of cognitive functions is hypothesized to be a manifestation of differential temporal dynamics in the neural structures and cognitive processors across the workspace.
source: We hypothesize that the differential temporal recovery of cognitive functions is a manifestation of differential temporal dynamics in the neural structures and cognitive processors across the workspace, which appear to return to, or be asymptotically close to, baseline approximately 3 hr after recovery of consciousness.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a hypothesis to explain the differential recovery.

claim: Hand squeezing to command is a simple, binary task unlike the more challenging cognitive battery with continuous performance measures such as accuracy and speed.
source: It is important to note that the first evidence of conscious access during recovery was hand squeezing to command, which is a simple, binary task unlike the more challenging cognitive battery with continuous performance measures such as accuracy and speed.
evidence: The discussion section distinguishes between the command-following task and the cognitive battery.

claim: Hand squeezing to command would not be robust evidence for a full reintegration of the global neuronal workspace.
source: Thus, hand squeezing to command would not be robust evidence for a full reintegration of the global neuronal workspace.
evidence: The discussion section interprets the command-following task in relation to workspace theory.

claim: Within 3 hours of recovery after a prolonged and deep general anesthetic, participants were performing a variety of complex cognitive tasks with similar accuracy and speed in comparison to participants who had not been anesthetized.
source: From a clinical perspective, it is remarkable that within 3 hr of recovery after a prolonged and deep general anesthetic, participants were performing a variety of complex cognitive tasks with similar accuracy and speed in comparison to participants who had not been anesthetized.
evidence: The discussion section emphasizes the clinical significance of the recovery findings.

claim: Both local and global dynamic measures of cortical activity returned to baseline levels just prior to the return of responsiveness after general anesthesia.
source: On a shorter timescale, both local and global dynamic measures of cortical activity returned to baseline levels just prior to the return of responsiveness after general anesthesia.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the EEG findings on a shorter timescale.

claim: There was no evidence of disrupted sleep in the days following anesthetic exposure compared to non-anesthetized controls.
source: On a longer timescale, there was no evidence of disrupted sleep in the days following anesthetic exposure compared to non-anesthetized controls.
evidence: The discussion section summarizes the actigraphy findings on a longer timescale.

claim: Actigraphy measures of sleep are sensitive to stress, low alcohol exposure, and even sedative effects of non-alcoholic beer.
source: This latter finding is striking considering that actigraphy measures of sleep are sensitive to stress, low alcohol exposure, and even sedative effects of non-alcoholic beer (Mezick et al., 2009; Geoghegan et al., 2012; Franco et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion section cites studies demonstrating the sensitivity of actigraphy.

claim: In healthy humans, higher cognition and arousal states recover uneventfully after deep general anesthesia.
source: The data suggest that, in healthy humans, higher cognition and arousal states recover uneventfully after deep general anesthesia.
evidence: The discussion section draws a conclusion about recovery in healthy humans.

claim: One study of healthy volunteers anesthetized with either propofol or dexmedetomidine found that those responsive to command exhibited activation of subcortical arousal centers with only limited frontal-parietal cortex involvement.
source: One study of healthy volunteers anesthetized with either propofol or dexmedetomidine and imaged using positron emission tomography found that those responsive to command exhibited activation of subcortical arousal centers with only limited frontal-parietal cortex involvement (Långsjö et al., 2012)
evidence: The discussion section cites a prior study for comparison.

claim: A recent study with a more sophisticated pharmacologic dosing strategy has largely confirmed findings of subcortical activation during emergence.
source: a recent study with a more sophisticated pharmacologic dosing strategy has largely confirmed these findings (Scheinin et al., 2021).
evidence: The discussion section cites a recent study confirming prior findings.

claim: A study of functional magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a transient activation of brainstem loci upon emergence from propofol sedation.
source: These data are consistent with a study of functional magnetic resonance imaging that demonstrated a transient activation of brainstem loci upon emergence from propofol sedation (Nir et al., 2019)
evidence: The discussion section cites a study demonstrating brainstem activation.

claim: A positron emission tomography study revealed subcortical and posterior cortical activation in association with the reversal of propofol sedation using the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor physostigmine.
source: as well as a positron emission tomography study revealing subcortical and posterior cortical activation in association with the reversal of propofol sedation using the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor physostigmine (Xie et al., 2011).
evidence: The discussion section cites a study on pharmacological reversal of sedation.

claim: All prior studies involved experimental conditions in which there was ongoing exposure to a sedative-hypnotic, coupled with pharmacological or behavioral stimulation.
source: However, it is important to note that all of these studies involved experimental conditions in which there was ongoing exposure to a sedative-hypnotic, coupled with pharmacological or behavioral stimulation.
evidence: The discussion section distinguishes the current study from prior studies.

claim: The current paradigm reflects spontaneous emergence with residual isoflurane levels predicted to be 1 to 4 orders of magnitude below those required for hypnosis.
source: By contrast, our paradigm reflects spontaneous emergence with residual isoflurane levels predicted to be 1 to 4 orders of magnitude below those required for hypnosis, which likely accounts for evidence of the robust return of cortical dynamics.
evidence: The discussion section describes the pharmacokinetic context of the current study.

claim: One animal study demonstrated that cholinergic stimulation of medial prefrontal cortex, but not two sites in posterior parietal cortex, was sufficient to reverse the anesthetized state despite continuous administration of clinically relevant concentrations of sevoflurane.
source: One animal study demonstrated that cholinergic stimulation of medial prefrontal cortex, but not two sites in posterior parietal cortex, was sufficient to reverse the anesthetized state despite continuous administration of clinically relevant concentrations of sevoflurane (Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion section cites an animal study on prefrontal cortex stimulation.

claim: The prefrontal cortex might play a critical role in recovery of both consciousness (medial prefrontal) and cognition (dorsolateral prefrontal).
source: Thus, the prefrontal cortex might play a critical role in recovery of both consciousness (medial prefrontal) and cognition (dorsolateral prefrontal).
evidence: The discussion section proposes a role for prefrontal cortex based on the findings.

claim: The study had surgically relevant anesthetic concentrations and duration of anesthetic exposure, in the absence of the confound of surgery itself.
source: Strengths of this study include: (1) surgically relevant anesthetic concentrations and duration of anesthetic exposure, in the absence of the confound of surgery itself
